text: You now know how to test hypotheses, build intervals, run regressions, and design experiments. This lesson is about the ways those tools go wrong even in careful hands. None of these mistakes need a bad intention — they come from how data and human attention behave, and each one can be demonstrated in a few lines of Python.

First: peeking at a running test. You launch an A/B test and check the p-value every day, stopping the moment it dips below 0.05. The trouble is every look is another chance for random noise to cross the line. Simulating an A-A test, where there's no true difference at all, with one planned look versus ten repeated looks.

With one planned look, about 4 to 5 percent of null experiments are flagged — close to the alpha of 0.05, as promised. With ten looks, about 20 percent are flagged. Fixed-sample tests are only valid when you look once, at the planned end. If you must monitor continuously, use a method built for sequential testing instead.

Second: Simpson's paradox. A trend in aggregated data can reverse when you split it into groups. Within desktop, treatment converts at 22 percent versus 20 percent. Within mobile, 5 percent versus 4 percent — treatment wins in both segments. Yet overall, treatment loses, 8.4 percent versus 16.8 percent, because most treatment users happened to be low-converting mobile visitors.

The cause is an uneven mix of segments across groups. A properly randomized test should balance device across arms, so an imbalance like this is a signal to investigate — and it's a constant hazard in observational data specifically.

Third: regression to the mean. If you select the extreme performers in one period, they tend to look less extreme the next period, even if nothing changes at all. Their first score was partly skill and partly luck, and luck doesn't repeat. The top decile scored 124.4 in year one and only 112.2 in year two, with zero intervention — if you'd applied a training program to that group, it would look like it added real value.

A few more traps. Hidden multiple comparisons — testing 20 metrics at alpha 0.05 gives about a 64 percent chance of at least one false positive. Survivorship bias — analyzing only the customers who stayed hides everyone who left. Base rate neglect — a 95 percent accurate test can still be wrong most of the time when what it detects is rare. And significant isn't important — with enough users, trivial effects reach p less than 0.05.

A habit checklist for every analysis: state the question and primary metric before looking at outcomes; fix sample size and stopping rule in advance; check group balance and sample sizes; report effect size with a confidence interval; count how many things you tested and correct for it; and ask what data is missing, and why.

To recap: most statistical errors aren't arithmetic — they're protocol errors. Peeking, ignoring segments, chasing extremes, and testing too many things. Building that checklist into your routine is worth more than any single test. Next, we build a full statistical analysis from start to finish in the capstone.
